title: companyDomainMismatch/implausibleCompany trust flags appear ~100% correlated with aggregator board, not with per-company evidence
body:
## Summary
In a 30-item ranked sample from `best-matches`, 12 of 12 aggregator-board (Adzuna) postings carry a negative trust flag (`companyDomainMismatch` on 11, `implausibleCompany` on 1), while 0 of 18 LinkedIn-board postings in the same sample carry either flag — including well-known, obviously legitimate companies (Saint-Gobain, Adecco, Bureau Veritas) on the LinkedIn side, and equally legitimate companies (Cisco, Dow, Colgate-Palmolive) on the flagged aggregator side.

## Reproduction
Sampled 30 ranked `best-matches` entries. Grouped by `board` and `trust.flags`:
- `board: aggregator` (12 entries): 11 with `companyDomainMismatch`, 1 with `implausibleCompany` — 12/12 flagged
- `board: linkedin` (18 entries): 0/18 flagged, all `trust.level: high`

Notably, real, verifiably legitimate companies (Cisco, Dow, Colgate-Palmolive, TD SYNNEX) are flagged simply for being sourced via the aggregator board, while the flag never fires for any LinkedIn-sourced posting in the sample, regardless of company legitimacy.

## Expected
A "company domain mismatch" flag should reflect genuine evidence about a specific listing/company (e.g. the apply-through URL's domain doesn't match the stated company's known domain), not the board a posting happened to be scraped from.

## Actual
The flag appears to fire deterministically based on board/source (very plausibly because Adzuna's own apply-URL structure always points through adzuna.it rather than the employer's domain, which would trivially and permanently trigger a same-domain-mismatch check for every single Adzuna-sourced listing regardless of the actual employer).

## Impact
Medium. If this hypothesis is correct, the flag currently carries no discriminating information for aggregator-board postings (it's constant, so it can't separate good listings from bad ones on that board) while appearing, to a user or any consumer, as if it were meaningful per-listing evidence. This could be masking genuinely suspicious listings on other boards, and unfairly downranking every legitimate Adzuna listing.

## Suggested direction (not prescriptive)
If the hypothesis holds, either exclude aggregator-sourced postings from this specific check (since the source URL pattern is expected/known, not suspicious), or compare against the *employer's* domain from the posting content rather than the apply-redirect URL.

_Filed from an Agent/MCP-based QA pass._

title: scrape_update_description is unusable via Agent/MCP: requires an internal id never exposed by any read command
body:
## Summary
`scrape_update_description` (a reversible, Agent/MCP-exposed command intended to let a caller correct a bad/missing scraped description) requires a `req.id` field. No read command available through the Agent/MCP surface (`job`, `best-matches`, `autopilot_best_matches`) ever returns an `id` for a posting — only `url` is exposed.

## Reproduction
1. Called `job` on a known posting URL — response contains `applied, board, clusterMembers, company, description, foundAt, isAgency, isNew, location, postedAt, score, scoreProvisional, scoreSource, title, trust, url`. No `id` field anywhere.
2. Called `scrape_update_description` with `{req: {id: <the same url>, description: "..."}}` (url used as a best-effort guess for id, since no real id is exposed).
3. Call returns success shape (`dispatched: true`) but `data: false`.
4. Re-read the same posting via `job` — description is unchanged from the original scraped text. The update silently did not apply.

## Expected
Either `scrape_update_description` should accept the `url` it's meant to correct (matching how every other read/write command in this session addresses postings), or the read commands should expose whatever `id` this command actually expects.

## Actual
The command cannot be driven to a successful, verified state via any combination of currently-exposed Agent/MCP data. `data: false` is also a silent no-op rather than an explicit "not found" error, making the failure easy to miss.

## Impact
Medium-high for anyone trying to fix known-bad descriptions programmatically (the exact workflow this session was attempting, based on the app's own established manual pattern of a user pasting a corrected LinkedIn description into the app). Currently only achievable through the GUI, if the GUI itself has access to the real id.

_Filed from an Agent/MCP-based QA pass._

title: LinkedIn-sourced postings systematically return empty description (6/6 sampled) while still scoring 100 / trust:high
body:
## Summary
Every LinkedIn-board posting checked this session (6 of 6, unrelated companies) has an empty `description` field, yet each still carries `score: 100`, `scoreSource: keyword`, and `trust: {level: high, flags: []}` — i.e. full confidence signals computed as if real content existed.

## Reproduction
Called `job` (by URL) on 6 separate LinkedIn postings found via normal autopilot discovery:
- Deix S.r.l. — "Business Developer & Growth Specialist"
- AIEM SRL — "Business Developer"
- Membrs — "Business Developer"
- Open Reply IT — "Business Developer"
- MEOTEC — "Business Development"
- Clinora Labs — "Business Development (BDR)"

All 6 return `"description": ""`. All 6 show `score: 100, trust.level: "high", trust.flags: []`.

## Expected
Either (a) description scraping succeeds for LinkedIn postings, or (b) when it fails, the resulting score/trust should reflect that the classification is based on title/metadata only, not full content — e.g. a lower confidence, a distinct flag, or exclusion from "high trust" until content is verified.

## Actual
Score and trust are computed and presented identically whether or not the underlying description was actually captured. A "100, high-trust" LinkedIn match is currently indistinguishable from a genuinely well-matched, fully-described posting.

## Impact
High. This is likely the single largest driver of wasted user time in the current matching pipeline — the highest-confidence-looking results are frequently the ones with no verifiable content behind them, and the UI/API gives no signal to tell the two apart.

## Suggested direction (not prescriptive)
A `descriptionMissing`/`descriptionLength` signal exposed alongside score, or a distinct trust flag (e.g. `descriptionUnavailable`) would let both the UI and any Agent/MCP consumer downrank or flag these appropriately without guessing.

_Filed from an Agent/MCP-based QA pass._

title: best-matches returns stale/pre-filter scores that don't reflect autopilot re-scoring
body:
## Summary
`best-matches` (and the `autopilot_best_matches` bridge command) return a cached `score`/`scoreProvisional` for a posting that does not reflect a subsequent re-score of that same posting after its sourcing autopilot's filter changed and re-ran. The live per-posting lookup (`job` command, by URL) shows the correct, current, much lower score for the same URL at the same moment.

## Reproduction
1. Autopilot "Business Development Milan" had `minMatchScore` raised to 50 and was re-run (confirmed via `autopilot_update` + a subsequent real run this session).
2. Called `best-matches` (global ranked view) — posting `https://www.adzuna.it/details/5827942629...` ("Business Development Manager Industries" @ CAP INGELEC) shows `score: 100.0, scoreProvisional: false`.
3. Called `job` directly on the exact same URL, same session, no intervening write to that record — returns `score: 17.0, scoreProvisional: true`.
4. Repeated with a second, unrelated posting (`.../5847861084`, "SEO Manager" @ Cerved): `best-matches` shows `score: 100.0`, `job` shows `score: 11.0, scoreProvisional: true`.

## Expected
`best-matches` should reflect the current authoritative score for a posting, or at minimum should not disagree with a direct per-posting lookup performed in the same session.

## Actual
Two independent postings show a large, contradictory score discrepancy (100 vs 11–17) between `best-matches` and `job`, with `best-matches` never reflecting the post-re-run, post-filter-change score.

## Impact
High. `best-matches` is the primary discovery surface (used by the app UI and by any Agent/MCP-driven workflow) — a user or agent triaging by this view will see a stale, misleadingly high score and waste time on postings that have already been correctly re-scored as poor matches internally. This directly undermines trust in the `minMatchScore` filtering feature, since its effect is invisible in the view users actually look at.

## Notes
- Both affected postings also turned out to be dead links (confirmed via live browser check), independent of this scoring issue.
- Not yet determined whether this is a caching layer that's never invalidated, or two genuinely separate score-storage paths that diverge. Flagging for engineering triage rather than diagnosing the root cause further from the Agent/MCP surface.

_Filed from an Agent/MCP-based QA pass._

title: fix: extension answer tools capture script and reasoning-aware draft budget
body:
## Why

The extension's AI answer tools were reported as flaky: "Help me answer" sometimes fails, and a rewrite with an instruction like "make it 200 characters" fails most of the time. Driving the real popup against the dev app, with the extension built from source and loaded into a scratch browser profile, found two defects, and neither was flakiness in the model.

## What

### The extension could never scan a filled form

Four injected scripts answer the background by their completion value: whatever the file's last statement evaluates to is what `executeScript` hands back. The per-entry build minified them, and Vite 8's minifier folded the trailing object literal in `capture.js` into two bare calls, so the completion value became the second call's array. The background rejected it, "Save my answers from this page" failed on every page with "Could not read the answers on this page", and because the rewrite picker is filled from that same scan, "Rewrite this answer" could never start. The store build, the 0.146.0 release zip and a fresh local build all carry the broken line.

The per-entry pass now builds unminified, its options are exported, turbo hashes the build config so a config change can no longer serve a cached dist, and a new test builds the real artifacts into a temp directory and asserts what each one evaluates to in a document with filled and empty fields. Turning minification back on fails that test on the capture script. The injected files grow from a few kilobytes to a few tens of kilobytes each, with their comments intact, which is also what add-on source review asks for.

### The draft budget was spent on reasoning

The bridge's draft and rewrite compose ran with an output budget of 1000 tokens and sent no reasoning effort. On a reasoning model the thinking counts against that budget. Measured live on Ollama Cloud gpt-oss:20b: "make it 200 characters" failed four times out of four, each time after about 3000 characters of thinking, with the stream ending on a length cut and no answer text; a plain "why do you want to work here" draft failed one time in four; presets that think for a few hundred characters always passed. The popup showed only "Could not draft an answer. Please retry."

The compose now asks for the cheapest reasoning tier the provider lists for the model, and only when that tier is minimal or low, so a model without one is unchanged. The budget is large enough to leave room for thinking on top of the visible answer, and it stays under the point where Anthropic's classic extended thinking would switch itself on, which is now a named predicate with a test on both sides of it. An empty length cut is retried exactly once at a larger budget, inside the same registered request: the registry entry is rebound rather than re-minted, so a cancel between the attempts can neither resurrect the request nor start a second billable job, the daily ceiling is charged per attempt, the client sees a single terminal frame, each attempt gets its own cap window over one append-only buffer so the wire is bounded by two attempts and never more, and the result carries only the text the successful attempt wrote.

## Verified live

Same harness, same model, after the fix: eleven of eleven calls succeeded and the retry was never needed. Four "make it 200 characters" rewrites came back at 215, 201, 183 and 202 characters. Two of those still used over 900 output tokens, so the old budget would have cut them. The lowest effort brought the drafts' thinking down from thousands of characters to about a hundred.

## Review history

Three internal rounds before this PR was opened, all findings verified against the code by a separate agent before anything was changed.

Round one found five real defects in the first fix, every one of them introduced by the fix itself: the retry re-registered the request under a fresh generation and leaked the first entry, a cancel landing between the attempts could start a billable job for an abandoned request, the failed first attempt emitted its own terminal frame, the build cache could serve a stale dist after a config change, and the budget crossed Anthropic's thinking threshold. Round two approved the rework and found, independently on all three critics, that the retry returned the shared buffer, so text the failed attempt had already forwarded rode back in front of the retry's answer. The strict pre-PR gate then caught two line-cap failures in the provider modules from the round-two doc comments, and that sharing the cap across attempts could silently cut a retry to a stub returned as success. Both are fixed here, with a security re-check of the cap change.

Advisory items left open on purpose, each recorded: the extension's stall timer is armed only by visible chunks while thinking is never forwarded, so a slow local model can look like a dead desktop across both attempts; the job registry marks the first attempt failed even when the retry succeeds; the narrow window between the registry read and the retry's daily charge is a documented coarse backstop; and the log-leak checker only matches `log::` macros, so the bridge's `tracing::` lines are outside it.

## Test plan

Extension: the new build-output test builds the four completion-value scripts with the shipping options and evaluates each against a fixture document; the capture case asserts the object shape and both arrays; re-enabling minification fails it. The existing extension suite passes.

Desktop: a fake composer whose first stream ends in an empty length cut is retried once at the larger budget and the low effort, the charge is counted twice, the result holds only the retry's text, each attempt is clamped at its own cap and the buffer keeps both; any other error is not retried; a cancelled request is refused a second charge; a registered request cannot be re-minted; exactly one terminal frame per request; a provider with no cheap tier sends no effort; the budget assertion sits next to the Anthropic predicate with its boundary pinned. Clippy locked with warnings as errors, the full lib suite, the architecture, egress and log-leak gates.

## Follow-ups (recorded, not done)

The extension gives up on a stream after 60 seconds without a visible chunk while the desktop allows 300, and thinking deltas are never forwarded, so a slow local model can still look like a dead desktop. The bridge's own informational log lines are filtered out at the shipped log level, which is why a failed draft leaves so little to read. Every published extension build carries the broken capture script, so users need a new store release to get the rewrite tools back.

title: [POC-2] Review Agent-Initiated Browser Navigation
body:
## POC-2 — Technical Review Request

### Scope
Agent-initiated navigation only:
`applications_open → open a stored application's job URL in a new background browser tab via the existing extension bridge`

No form filling and no submission capability were added or attempted.

### Implementation status
POC-2 is implemented in an isolated local worktree and has never been pushed.

Implemented:
- `NAVIGATE_REQUEST` / `NAVIGATE_RESULT` protocol
- Rust wire constants and shared TypeScript protocol types
- `applications_open` command with `Effect::Reversible`
- bridge correlation registry
- extension handler using `browser.tabs.create({ url, active: false })`

### Verified
- TypeScript typecheck: clean
- Extension tests: 588/588 passing across 14 files
- Zero test regressions

### Unverified / blocker
Rust/Tauri compilation could not be completed.

Root cause was confirmed precisely using `vswhere.exe`: Visual Studio Build Tools 2019 is installed, but the C++/MSVC workload was never installed. `cl.exe` and `link.exe` are absent from the machine.

Therefore this is currently a machine environment blocker, not evidence that the POC-2 Rust source changes fail to compile.

Because the binary could not be built, the real E2E test:
`Agent → App → Extension → browser.tabs.create({ active:false })`
could not be executed.

### Safety design
The implementation remains intentionally constrained:
- HTTPS-only
- Requested URL must exactly match the application's stored `job_url`
- Opens a new background tab with `active:false`
- Does not touch the user's active tab
- No generic browser-control API
- No `applications_submit` capability
- No automatic form submission
- `submitDetected` remains observational only

The intended workflow stops at `READY_TO_SUBMIT`; the user manually performs the final Submit action.

### Isolation
Nothing has been:
- deployed to the live app
- deployed to the live extension
- pushed
- merged
- submitted as a PR
- installed on the system
- changed in system configuration

### Review requested
Please review the POC-2 architecture and security model, especially:
1. `applications_open` design
2. App → Extension navigation protocol
3. Exact `job_url` matching and HTTPS validation
4. Background-tab behavior via `tabs.create({ active:false })`
5. Absence of any Agent-side submission capability
6. Whether this architecture is appropriate to proceed to build verification and E2E testing

No further implementation should be started until this review is complete.
